text: Dana Angluin is a professor emeritus of computer science at Yale University. She is known for her foundational contributions to computational learning theory and distributed computing. Angluin earned her B.A. in 1969 and Ph.D. in 1976 from the University of California, Berkeley. Her doctoral thesis, titled "An application of the theory of computational complexity to the study of inductive inference," was one of the first works to apply complexity theory to inductive inference. She joined the Yale faculty in 1979. Her research helped establish the theoretical foundations of machine learning. She developed the L* algorithm, which enables learning of regular language sets from membership and equivalence queries, using a minimally adequate teacher (MAT) that provides yes-or-no answers to membership and equivalence queries. The Learner refines its understanding of the unknown set in polynomial time based on these responses. Although the paper was published in 1987, a 2017 article by Frits Vaandrager notes that the most efficient learning algorithms currently in use follow Angluin's approach of a minimally adequate teacher. Her work on learning from noisy examples has also been highly influential, demonstrating the existence of algorithms that can learn despite errors in training data. In distributed computing, she co-invented the population protocol model and studied consensus. She has also researched randomized algorithms for Hamiltonian circuits and matchings. Angluin helped found the Computational Learning Theory (COLT) conference and has served on its program and steering committees. She served as an area editor for Information and Computation from 1989 to 1992 and organized Yale's Perlis Symposium in April 2001, titled "From Statistics to Chat: Trends in Machine Learning." She is a member of the Association for Computing Machinery and the Association for Women in Mathematics. Angluin is highly celebrated as an educator, having received three of Yale College's most distinguished teaching prizes: the Dylan Hixon Prize for Teaching Excellence in the Sciences, the Bryne/Sewall Prize for distinguished undergraduate teaching, and the Phi Beta Kappa DeVane Medal. She has also published works on Ada Lovelace and her involvement with the Analytical Engine.
